maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as one of those who have taken up very little time of the committee, I should like to say a few words in connection with the operation and leadership of the Royal Canadian Air Force. I have for various reasons been very much interested in this branch of the service, no doubt due to the faet that I know so many young men of the force who have paid the supreme sacrifice and many others who also are ready to give everything they have to defend our country in this fight for freedom and justice.
Let me pause for just one moment to offer my hearty congratulations to the minister of National Defence for Air upon his splendid speech on the floor of this house, as reported at pages 3723 and 3724 of Hansard of June 26, 1942. With such leadership the Royal Canadian Air Force is bound to fly at a very high altitude.
The Royal Canadian Air Force is one of Canada's chief sources of pride in our whole war effort. It is composed of young men who are among the finest in the land. In many theatres of war its members have brought glory to themselves and to their country and will continue to do so in even greater measure

War Appropriation-Air Services
as the war becomes more intense in the final struggle on the continent of Europe and elsewhere.
I was very much interested in receiving information that I asked for with regard to the number of decorations awarded to men in the Royal Canadian Air Force who were enlisted or appointed in Toronto, and I should like to put the numbers of these decorations on Hansard so that they may be on record. Decorations have been awarded to men enlisted or appointed in Toronto as follows:
Order of the British Empire	 1
Distinguished Service Order	 1
Distinguished Flying Cross	 44
Air Force Cross	 4
Distinguished Flying Medal	 16
Air Force Medal	 2
British Empire Medal	 1
"Mention"	 13
"Commendation"	 6
Knowing a number of these young men who have won such honourable distinction, is it any wonder, Mr. Chairman, that I should give high praise to the service? I am sure that all hon. members will agree with me that there is very little criticism that can be applied to this branch of our armed forces. Everywhere you go you hear nothing but the highest praise of the Royal Canadian Air Force, and what has been said along that line by speakers who have preceded) me is a good example for the rest of us to follow.
May I make one or two suggestions to the minister which I believe will meet with widespread approval? It is hard to say that all young men in the aircrews are of officer material, but what I should like to see is that all members of the aircrews be placed together in the use of a common mess as is the custom in the far and middle east.
I should also like to offer a suggestion in connection with the rehabilitation of the Royal Canadian Air Force personnel. This would, I believe, be a fitting conclusion to a glorious incident in Canada's air history. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I will read what I have prepared in this connection.

1.	The question of rehabilitation of R.C.A.F. personnel is a matter which deserves not only the best thought that is possible on the particular question, but also that this thought should be initiated immediately. The success of any rehabiliation measures will depend on having them determined in all their different aspects before rehabilitation, on any large scale, becomes necessary.
2.	The rehabilitation of air force personnel, more particularly aircrew, has certain special features, namely:
(i)	Air force personnel, more particularly aircrew, are men and women of a high level of educational standing.
(ii)	Aircrew will have been through emotional experiences which will have given them a maturity beyond their years.
(iii)	The majority of aircrew personnel will be young men in their early twenties who have a good educational background but no special vocational experience.
(iv)	The rehabilitation of women personnel will be a particular problem in so far as there will be many young women of good educational background who have interrupted their educational and vocational training to enter the air force.
3.	There is at present within the air force an organization for the repatriation of air force personnel. It is submitted, however, that this organization must of necessity be confined entirely to the routine of arrangements for discharge of personnel. There must be a separate organization for the rehabilitation of air force personnel.
4.	It is suggested that there should be established within the air force some kind of organization to provide facilities for air force personnel who are to be repatriated or discharged' to enable them to do some serious thinking about their future vocation.
5.	It is suggested further that the educational directorate of the air force should be so organized as to undertake immediately the whole question of rehabilitation, whereby facilities could be provided to give air force personnel who are to be repatriated or' discharged, vocational guidance and an opportunity to pursue the necessary educational courses required for their future vocations. Aircrew personnel, who are to be repatriated or discharged, will require this vocational guidance during the period (in the service) in which they are being emotionally restored towards future civilian life. It will be the responsibility of the Royal Canadian Air Force to give this vocational guidance. Furthermore, it is submitted that there will be no better therapeutic measures for these young men than to stimulate in them healthy thoughts about their future vocations.
6.	The answer to rehabilitation is a job, and it should be the responsibility of the air force to provide any necessary educational training to enable air force personnel to get this job. Also it is realized that there will be in the air force personnel who return many

War Appropriation-Air Services
of the best brains of Canada. The majority of these brilliant young men will have interrupted their education. It is the responsibility of the air force to direct the thoughts of these boys to the furtherance of their higher education and to dissuade them, as will be necessary in many cases, from breaking away from their early pre-war intentions of a university career.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that this job of rehabilitation can best be done by those in charge of the building of the Royal Canadian Air Force. In conclusion, may I say: Carry on, Royal Canadian Air Force.

Mr. Chairman, it would be almost redundant for me to add a humble tribute to the administration of the Department of National Defence for Air, but I am very glad to do so because I believe that the minister has given it his very best attention; he has accepted criticism where it was due, and he has never paraded the Royal Canadian Air Force or the British commonwealth air training plan as a perfect model, but has endeavoured at every turn to improve it where improvement was required. I hope that any suggestions which may come from this side he will take in that spirit as he has done in the past, for he is assured in his heart, and he knows it without anyone saying it, that there is nothing which any member of this house and any member of the Canadian public will not do to further the interests of these men over whom he has charge.
I do not think the people of Canada fully realize the debt of gratitude which they owe to the men who serve in the aircrew of the Royal Canadian Air Force, to say nothing of the men who served with the Royal Air Force and fought in the battle of Britain and in all the battles which have been waged since that time. I shall not say that the failure to realize exactly what the air force has done for us is because of poor publicity; it may be due to the fact that the air raids are now so constant, and the air battles in the past were of such frequency, that we do not realize the significance of each of these air raids which takes place.
Let us consider for a moment what is meant to Canada when an air raid of 600 planes takes place on any one of these evenings which we are now passing through. With an average crew of say eight to a plane, that means 4,800 men. Every night we have, in the number of aircrew going over Germany, a force equivalent to that which took part in the raid on Dieppe. That is something we do not realize on account of the great frequency of these air raids. And, so that we may realize how large
[Mr. Hoblitzell.J
a share is Canada's in these air raids, no less than a quarter of the aircrews that take part in the raids are R.C.A.F. personnel, serving with the Royal Canadian Air Force and Royal Air Force, and for good measure we can add another five per cent of Canadians who enlisted in Royal Air Force units. Only a few nights ago, fifty-seven of the casualties reported were boys of our own country, our own brothers and sons.
Whether anything can be done to bring the realization of this great contribution more vividly to the general public apart from those whose actual relations are engaged in it I do not know, but I feel that if it is possible to give greater publicity to the individual exploits, as well as the exploits of the corps, it should be done. I believe that the minister, if he is of the same opinion as he was last year, will agree that we must give all the personal tribute that we can, because we on this side of the Atlantic at least are used to having heroes, and it is a great inspiration to the young men serving in the force and to those who are likely to enlist to know that they have a chance of getting this glory personally, as well as serving in the common cause.
I am also glad to know the minister feels that we may make very considerable progress in the winning of this war through bombing operations alone. He shares, I think, the view of the Prime Minister of Great Britain when he says that it is something well worth trying, as long as we do not forget the other arms of the service.
One point which has been mentioned already and which will find, I believe approval among all parties of this house, is in connection with the granting of commissions and the withholding of the same to aircrew. It is an invidious distinction which grew out of the tail-end of the last war. I remember it very well, because at that time I was a boy of seventeen and I was in the Royal Air Force, as it was called then. I can remember lining up with the other young recruits, and a young lieutenant there simply picked some of us to be cadets for pilots, which meant a commission, and others to be sergeant-pilots, without any preliminaries at all. It did seem an unfair way, because those who had special influence might be able to change their position afterwards. But the distinction between commissioned officers and non-commissioned sergeants, all of whom were to serve as aircrew, grew out of the end of the last war and apparently was carried over into this war. I do not see that

War Appropriation-Air Services
it has any relation at all to Canadian soil; it may have something to do with other countries, but certainly it is entirely foreign to Canada, and I do not think we want to see any of it here.
It is quite true, on the other hand, that if the only consideration in granting a commission is grades in the courses, those who do better than others are perhaps entitled to rewards, as in other walks of life. Nevertheless, when the men are serving together in the same aircraft there is an invidious distinction, which I think should be done away with. It was suggested by one of my colleagues that it might be better to adopt the United States system of appointment of aircrew to become flight officers with the equivalent of warrant officer's rank, and subsequently they could earn their commissions. I am not positive on that point, but I have heard it said that that is the way in which the matter is handled there. Certainly, the man who graduates as a member of an aircrew is entitled to some rank which, I think, should be at least that of warrant officer; and upon proof of service, not necessarily operations over Europe but including good service in the corps, he should be entitled to rank for his commission.
As I understand it, the system in practice works that only the top third of the graduating classes are granted commissions and the remainder become sergeant pilots. Now that Canada has a larger number of R.C.A.F. establishments and is paying for the same, the old reason of being influenced by joint costs, because Great Britain was paying a good part of the shot of the increased remuneration which officers would get, has to a large extent gone. We are running our own show to a considerable extent, and we should be able to call our own tune with regard to creating officers or not. I understand that a sergeant-pilot or an aircrew sergeant must be recommended by his commanding officer for a commission, or he may apply, under certain rules, for a commission. I should like to trespass on the privilege of the house and read from the agreement in connection with the air training plan dated at Ottawa, June 5, 1942, which I think is the last agreement. This is "Conditions of service of air crews, R.C.A.F. pupils."
1. Commissioning- . . .
(a)	All pilots, observers, navigators and air bombers who are considered suitable according to the standards of the government of Canada and who are recommended for commissions will be commissioned.
I do not see any limitation in the clause to one-third, which I understand is the practice.

On graduation, of course.
(b)	The percentages of commisisons given at the date of this agreement to wireless operator-air gunners, namely twenty per cent of total graduates, divided ten per cent on graduation and ten per cent after service, and air gunners, namely twenty per cent of total graduates, divided five per cent on graduation and fifteen per cent after service, will be maintained.
I might ask the committee to bear in mind, with regard) to these percentages after service, that from what information I have it does not appear that the chances of being promoted afterwards are very much better than theoretical. Actually the total who have been promoted after failing to get their commissions upon graduation has not been very great.
Then:
Some flexibility will, however, be permitted to ensure that airmen in these categories who have the necessary qualifications are not excluded from commissions on account of the quota.
Well, according to the minister the quota has gone except perhaps as to the air gunners, et cetera.

(c)	Normally, the initiative in recommending an airman for a commission will rest with his commanding officer, but an airman may apply to be recommended, and, if his application is endorsed and forwarded by his commanding officer, it will receive the same consideration as if it had been initiated by the latter.
Namely, the commanding officer.
An application for a commission by an airman of the Royal Canadian Air Force, even if it is not endorsed, will be forwarded through the usual channels to R.C.A.F. overseas headquarters. The headquarters will be provided with all relevant documents and will arrange for the candidate to appear before a selection board convened by the air officer-in-chief, R.C.A.F. overseas.
In regard to that clause, I would ask the minister if what is there indicated exists anywhere at all except om paper-

speechtext:
You bet.

-and if it does, I should like to know whether there is any substantial number of men, and how many, who have actually received1 commissions in that way.

speechtext: What clause is it?

speechtext: Would the hon. member be good enough to repeat that? I want to get it more accurately.

I understand that there are some members of the Royal Canadian Air Force ground crew who would be fit as fighting men in the army, and at the same time the army has among its ranks those who are not fit for combatant service, low category men who would be good material for ground crew. Could an exchange be made? The suggestion has been made that the minister might not care for that idea, but there is nothing wrong with some of these men, and, after all, valuable as the services of the ground crew are,

War Appropriation-Air Services
such service is not quite as irreplaceable as that of front-line fighting men. I think the minister appreciates the point.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Does the hon. member think the ground crew in North Africa, in Ceylon and in the middle east are not fighting men?
The other day I understood the minister to say that the ground crew overseas is relatively small-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I rather object to the hon. member saying that the ground crew are not fighting men. We have in North Africa, in Ceylon and in the middle east men who are as much fighters as the men in any other service.
I confine myself to the ground crew within Canada.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Or in Great Britain?
We are bound to have a very great number of ground crew men who must be kept here to look after training requirements of the joint plan.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I tell my hon. friend I am not going to have an organization of cripples.
I am not suggesting that the minister should.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I tell you that right now.

I do not suppose the minister imagines for a moment that I would press the matter so far.
May I ask the minister also if there was anything in the suggestion that was made in a newspaper about a fleet of air arm being formed? Surely that is not due to any suggestion of inability or inefficiency on the part of his colleagues, or otherwise, or that the Royal Canadian Air Force cannot look after patrol. It was a news item that appeared once and perhaps it was not official; nevertheless it was there. I understand that the fleet air arm in Britain is confined to aircraft carriers, and so far as I know, we have no aircraft carriers here.
The minister might also throw some light on the stores and equipment depots. I often wonder, when I see the tremendous equipment depot at the foot of Yonge street in Toronto, which has been filled for years with parts, what becomes of outmoded material. Have the old materials been moved out for replacement and their places taken by new materials so that the equipment in the various depots is fairly modern, or has any substantial part of these materials become entirely outmoded? I should not blame the minister if it has, because there have been great and rapid changes in connection with aircraft.
Then a question with regard to the Cana-d'ianization of the Royal Canadian Air Force. As we have seen from agreements which the minister has tabled, this Canadianization has gone on somewhat apace during the last year.
I think the minister stated that in order to have sufficient ground crew to service our aircrew we should require something over 200,000 men. Obviously that would be impossible. Therefore we cannot hope to complete the total Canadianization of our air crew in the near future or perhaps during this war. It might not be practicable. However, as the hon. member for Calgary East mentioned, there are still some Canadians in the R.A.F who enlisted prior to or at the outbreak of the war. These men went over to Great Britain after, in some instances, taking some preliminary training here, and enlisted with the R.A.F. I do not know how numerous they are, but from time to time I have met Canadians in this category. The minister will probably have fairly exact figures.
Have these men been given an opportunity to re-muster into the R.C.A.F.? I think it was stated last year that some of these men had become so attached to the R.A.F. service that they did not want to change over, but I think they should be given an opportunity to re-muster, not only because they would be with their fellow-Canadians, but for other very practical reasons. There is not only the difference in pay between the English and the Canadian rates, but a Canadian in the R.A.F. is obliged to pay the British income tax. I was told by a Canadian squadron leader serving with the R.A.F. that after deductions his pay was equivalent to that received by a pilot officer in the R.CA.F. who was serving in the same squadron in England. On the surface this seems to be an absurd situation.
In connection with pensions our government has seen fit to give Canadians serving in the Royal Air Force the Canadian rate of pension. So far as I can discover from the agreements, the primary responsibility for this pension is still upon the United Kingdom government rather than the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Those men are not covered by any agreement we have made with the United Kingdom. They have nothing to do with it at all.

Group 3 consists of a very much smaller number of personnel who, under certain recruiting offers which were made in Canada by the R.A.F. prior to the war, enlisted . . .

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am sorry, but I understood my hon. friend to be speaking of the air training agreement made in Junev of last year. The men who enlisted with the Royal Air Force before the war have not been covered by any agreement made by National Defence for Air of Canada with the air ministry. We have had nothing to do with them in so far as pensions are concerned.

They are covered by the Pension Act. It was probably the minister's colleague who handled that. We have undertaken to see that those Canadians who enlisted with the Royal Air Force before the war shall get the same treatment, and I wish to make sure that this is not just a privilege which is being given to them, but a right.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It was granted by this parliament, so that I take it to be a right.

It would be so under the Pension Act.
There are one or two matters upon which I hope the minister can throw some light. One is in connection with the appropriation of $93,000,000 this year for works and buildings. As the minister suggested in his opening speech, less building is being done this year. The whole air training plan has been set up, and it is now simply a matter of turning the wheels and getting production. Yet the overhead in connection with works and buildings appears to be maintained. I should like to ask the minister, when the time comes-it must be the same in this department as in many others-for a specific reduction to take place, just how the reduction will come about. There is always a reluctance to disturb a situation which is functioning.
Another word in regard to organization. I think one reason why the Royal Canadian Air Force has made such tremendous strides and achievements is the fact that it was a new service. At the beginning of the war the number of personnel in the permanent force was not sufficiently large to clutter up the machinery, nor was it sufficiently large to stop the wheels of progress, as some of us think has taken place in some of the older services. Adequate recognition has been given to personnel which did not see any great future in the air force in peace time, but did see a future in business, to which they applied their abilities. These abilities have been transferred to the air force and they have received the appropriate recognition. I think the minister has been wise to make sure of any contribution, no matter where it comes from, whether from new blood or from the old Royal Military College type if you like, and to give it due recognition.

Nevertheless, as your organization matures, things tend to become static, and you find new jobs for people who are simply performing functions which were performed by some of the old personnel. For instance, I understand that at one of the training centres the personnel is about double what it was in 1941, whereas the output of pilots has not changed at all. This tendency to increase overhead is common to all organizations, as the minister knows, and I believe he would1 want to check any growth along this line.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Would my hon. friend mind giving me privately the name of that particular station, so that I may check this matter?

I shall be glad to do so.
There are a few smaller matters I should like to mention, but perhaps they can be raised more appropriately on the various items. I only hope that the minister will continue to make the progress and achieve the success with the R.C.A.F. that he has in the past, and that our boys overseas will continue the glorious work they have been carrying oni in the past.

I shall not take the time of the committee to assure the minister of what he knows already, that all Canada is very proud of his boys in the air force and that by now I judge Germany and the countries under German domination have learned to fear them. I have a personal interest in the men in the air force, because more than three hundred boys from' my classes and fifteen of the teachers with whom I worked before coming to the house are now in this force.
There are three matters I should like to call to the minister's attention. While the first may not be within the scope of these estimates, it has been referred to already and I am sure it will interest the minister. I wish to speak, as the hon. member for Calgary East and others have done, for our Canadian boys who are in the Royal Air Force. I know some of those boys who went to England on cattle-boats during the depression years, when they could find' no employment in this country; who signed six-year contracts with the Royal Air Force and who were among the first Canadian boys to see active service in the air when war broke out. Practically all our legislation with regard to returned men and their rehabilitation provides that Canadians in the Royal Air Force or other branches of the services of the allied nations shall receive the same treatment as those in the Canadian forces, subject to the provision that

War Appropriation-Air Services
they must have been domiciled in Canada at the time of enlistment. Those boys, probably together with others in other branches of the service, were not domiciled in Canada at the time of their enlistment. Some of them are writing home now asking what their status will be when the war is over. I have been in communication with the Minister of Pensions and National Health on this question, and he assures me it is the intention of his department to see that those boys are brought within the scope of the legislation providing for rehabilitation. But unless this matter can be cleared up now, before those boys come home, it is quite possible that when the war is over, grounds may be found for excluding them from some of the benefits to which the boys in the Canadian forces will be entitled. Therefore I would suggest to the Minister of National Defence for Air and to the ministers of the other service departments that steps be taken now, before those boys come back, to see that their position after the war is clarified, so that there may be no doubt that they are entitled to whatever rehabilitation benefits are provided for the boys in the Canadian forces.
There is one other point of a similar nature to which I wish to direct the minister's attention; I imagine later on it will probably come under the administration of the Department of Labour. I refer to the matter of education interrupted by the war. A number of boys have written me wanting to know just what is meant by education interrupted by the war. I should like to impress upon the minister the fact that the training and educational advantages that have been given the boys in the air force, and the training that has been given the boys in the other branches of the service, have given many of them a new realization of the value of education. A great many of the boys who will return from overseas, who had very little interest in education before going into the armed forces, will be desirous of continuing their education, regardless of the point at which that education was interrupted. We shall find that many boys who did not finish their high-school education, who probably never gave any indication of any intention to enter university, will, in all probability, when they return, want to complete their high school education and to be given the privilege of entering a university. I have discussed this matter with the educational officers of the air force and army, and the consensus among them is that any boy who returns from the war should be given
the privilege of taking up his education where he left off, without being asked to show that before he enlisted he intended to go through high school or on to a university or some other educational institution. I think in the interests of the future of this country we should provide for the boys who return from overseas any educational opportunities which they desire and of which they can make use. It will be of benefit to the boys now in the forces if some statement can be made clarifying just what is meant by that term, the continuation of education interrupted by the war.
I have one other matter which comes within the scope of the first item, which deals with civil salaries and wages. A year ago I was in communication with the minister concerning the wages paid to civilian employees at some of the air force camps.
I understood then that steps were being or had been taken to improve this condition, and I have received information to the effect that the condition which prevailed a year ago has been considerably improved. But there are some of those camps in which veterans of the great war are employed as civilians at what I still consider very low wages.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If I may ask my hon. friend a question in connection with the class of labour to which he refers, are not those men employed at the prevailing rates in the different localities, as fixed by the Department of Labour? That was my impression, and I should like to know if that is the situation.

Here is one concrete example. A great war veteran employed at I.T.S. No. 5 near Belleville tells me that he receives $50 a month plus $1 a day subsistence allowance, giving him less than an average of $20 a week in all. The camp is situated at some distance from the city, and transportation costs most of the men going to that camp sixty cents a week. I do not know what the minister thinks, but to me that is a pretty low wage. I gather from the letter of this man that he has a fairly responsible position in the camp.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Unless the hon. gentleman has some other information I can only suggest that this rate of wages must be fixed either by the Department of Labour or by the civil service commission. I am quite sure that must be the situation, because we do not fix the rates of wages for this work.

I do not know who fixes it, but I would say that wage is too low for a man of that calibre.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think it is very high.

This may not be the responsibility of the minister, but it is a matter which does affect men employed in his organization, and if he has any responsibility in the matter I would suggest that some adjustment should be made.

I do not rise on this occasion to condemn or even to advise, but I do not wish this opportunity to pass without paying, on behalf of my riding of Renfrew North, a tribute to the Royal Canadian Air Force and the commonwealth air training plan. Sometimes I think we are inclined to forget the great background of the air training plan. We are inclined to forget the enormous amount of work that went into the setting up of the plan, before it finally got under way. We are told that originally the plan called for seventy-four air training schools dotted1 here andi there across Canada, and that it was later enlarged to 154. Can anyone imagine the amount of work that went into the locating of those air training fields, right across the country? Can we properly understand the work involved in finding the right locations, and in surveying them? That work was done by the Department of Transport. It was a work which must have involved a great deal of effort and organization on the part of the officials of that department.
Then the Department of Munitions and Supply was called in to get the fields in order, to let contracts for the grading of land', the erection of buildings, the laying of pipelines, the supplying of water, the disposal of sewage and the installation of plumbing. All this involved a tremendous effort, one we are apt to forget about. It was accomplished, not only by the officials of that department but also with the aid of a great army of civilian labourers. They accomplished a magnificent amount of work in the preparation of these air training schools.
I believe the minister said that approximately 50,000 airmen who go aloft have been trained under the plan. That is surely an accomplishment of which we may be proud. A great amount of education is involved in the training of a pilot, an observer, an air gunner or any of the personnel who fly.
Sometimes I stop to think why those boys wanted to get into the air force. In the early days of the war the boys who complained to me were those who wanted to join the air force, and who did- not know why they should

not be accepted at once. They were clamouring to join, knowing all the time that a pilot, observer or air gunner must be trained to a high degree of perfection. They knew, too, that they had to be almost perfect physically and mentally, and that the educational standards were high.
I believe I heard the minister say on one occasion that possibly he had spoiled our young men who entered the air force. But he said he deliberately set out to do that, because he wanted the cream of the country. He set out to pay them well, to feed them well and to treat them well. He stated further that his plan worked, and that he got what he wanted. Even to-day boys from my constituency are still on the waiting list, and still clamouring to join the air force.
I presume one reason why they prefer the air service is that they know they will see action, and that the air force has been in the front line during a time when the army has had to wait. When a civilian decides to go to war he prefers to go at once, get the fighting over and be done with it. They want action, and our boys knew that if they were taken into the air force they would find plenty of action. They have covered themselves with glory in all parts of the world. I pick at random clippings from my home town of Pembroke, and I find that they record the deeds of many of our boys in all parts of the world'-Egypt, Africa, Tunisia. They are here and there across the world. They are fighting, winning medals for their valour, doing splendid work and bringing glory to their country and to themselves.
There is another reason, however, why the boys want to see action. This was put beautifully in a letter written by a North Bay boy to his mother. It is contained in a newspaper article bearing the North Bay dateline of April 17, as follows:
Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Boyer have just received a letter written by their son, Fit. Sgt. A. B. Boyer, R.C.A.F., who was killed in action overseas, last October.
The letter was written last July and handed to a chaplain to forward in event of his death. It says: "I am writing this week in ease I get killed, because if I did get killed I would want you to know why. It's because I have always loved you very much and I came over here, as all other Canadian did, to stop Hitler from going to Canada and doing harm to you."
That is very touching, and just the language a boy would use. I think he is right in saying that the motive in the minds and hearts of our young men, when they offered themselves to perform this dangerous task, was that they were thinking of their loved ones. They felt they had a duty to perform, a job to do, and they did not hesitate to do it.

War Appropriation-Air Services
I pay tribute to those boys of ours who have gone in that spirit to do their work, a work they are doing so magnificently and so well.
While I am on my feet may I pay tribute to the mothers who have given those splendid boys to this task. Some of the boys will not return to the mothers who gave them to their country. In those cases the mothers' hearts will be terribly broken. In other cases boys may learn in foreign lands that during their absence their mothers have gone to a better land. But they should not worry unduly. While the mothers are here, they pray unceasingly for the welfare of their boys. Their thoughts go with them; they live with them. But if they are taken, they go to a better land, and then I feel the mothers may be in an even better position to stay close to those boys to protect and care for them. I am going to put on.record a poem written by Edna Jaques of Toronto which I think sums up the feeling of the mothers of the boys of the air force in most beautiful language:
"Son's Going Away"
Nobody mourns them as mothers do Nobody watches and waits and weeps,
Love forgets and the world goes by But mothers sorrow and pray and keep Little bits of him treasured up His old school sweater-his hockey cup.
Never a day goes by or a night
But she visions him in a hundred ways
He lives in the night, in the wind and stars,
He is part of her, and the weary days Go empty save for her dreams of him Brave as a lion, stalwart, slim.
She rides with him in his shining plane Over the channel upon a raid Sharing the cockpit, charting trails,
Flying his Spitfire, unafraid.
Prays for his safety, day and night _ Upholding him by her love's sheer might.
Nobody mourns him as mothers do Horning-evening-sunset and dawn Love forgets and the world goes by But mothers keep faith when hope is gone, Steady and true as the stars above Nothing can touch it-a mother's love.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think there is anyone in the house or outside it who does not appreciate the work the air force is doing, and certainly no one underestimates the responsibility which these young fellows will have to assume in the very near future, to say nothing of the splendid work they have been doing up to the present. As time goes on, I think we shall realize that the air force is bound to become more important than perhaps any other branch of the armed forces. But there is one thing I would point out to the minister. In view of the fact that the air force will be called upon to render greater service as time
goes on, and there will be a greater number of air force casualties too, we have not in my opinion expanded the air force as much as we should have done in Canada. From my experience in travelling over the country I believe that the air force is not being expanded as rapidly as it could and should be.
We have in Canada at the present time more training aircraft than the air force can use. I remember talking to an officer in one of the air force training centres, and I asked him if that was a fact. He told me that they wyere training men just as fast as they could with the facilities they had at hand. I said, "What do you mean? Have you not enough space here for landing fields, or buildings?" He said, "That is not necessarily the cause of our not training more men. The point is, we really have not enough planes." I drew his attention to the fact that we had in storage in Canada large numbers of training planes which were not being used. It seems to me that this condition of affairs should not exist. I know we should keep a sufficient number of planes in reserve in case of smashes or crashes and a sufficient supply of parts for repairs. But when this officer told me that they were not training any more men because they did not have the aircraft, that did not just jibe with what I knew to be the fact. My information is that we have more training planes available than the air force is using, and that as fast as the air force wants to expand the Minister of Munitions and Supply can supply the planes required if they would only order them. But I think the practice is that the Department of Munitions and Supply makes no move in regard to supplying planes unless the air force orders them.
That brings me to another point. I would ask the minister how it is possible for a man in the army to transfer to the air force. I believe that is being done. I recall that over a year ago a young fellow who was in the army in England wrote to me and wanted to know how he could get into the air force. That had been his goal ever since he enlisted, about six months after the war started. He was eager to get into the fighting forces and his choice was the air force, but he was advised at that time to join the army and that he would then have no difficulty in transferring over to the air force. He spent all his training time with the army here in Canada; then was sent over to England and was there for a year when he wrote me asking how he could get into the air force. I took the question up with the Department of National Defence and was informed by the department what steps he

War Appropriation-Air Services
should take. I accordingly wrote and told him what he should do. He did that, and then about two months ago I received another letter from him saying that he had not got into the air force but still had hopes of getting there. I would ask the minister how that can be done.
I also wish to bring to the minister's attention a case that came before me about three weeks ago. I would ask the minister, is a young fellow in the air force on the day he is sworn in? My information is that this young fellow was sworn into the air force on July 16. Then he was sent home on leave without pay. Was he in the air force on the day he was sworn in, or was he in the air force after he was called back from being on leave without pay? I should like the minister to settle that point, because it so happens that later on this boy developed a sickness and upon his discharge the question arose as to when he was in the air force.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will look into the matter. Roughly I would say this. If he developed a sickness while on leave without pay and had not participated in any way in the work of the air force, I would hate to say that I would be responsible for him.
He did1 not develop the sickness while on leave without pay. He came back from leave and was in the air force for four or five months.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend will have to discuss that with the department of pensions. He certainly was in the air force if he served in the air force and was actually a member of the air force. But the question of responsibility for pension or compensation or what have you, is one for the board1 of pension commissioners and is not for the decision of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
Would he be considered on strength the day he was sworn in on July 16?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not see how that question would arise if the beginning of the illness or disability occurred when he was a member of the air force. If my hon. friend would send1 me particulars-
I think the whole thing hinges on whether he was on the strength the day he was sworn in.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will let
me have the particulars I shall be only too glad to hand the case over to pensions to get an opinion.

I have
already taken the case up with some of their officials but have not got very far. The whole case hinges on whether the man was on the strength the day he was sworn in.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am quite certain the hon. member cannot get very far with me to-night because I would have to see all the particulars.
Surely the minister could say whether a person-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The minister will not give
a decision on a pension case. He never did it even when he was Minister of Pensions, and he is not going to start it now, when he is out of the job.
I am not asking the minister to decide on a pension case. All I am asking is, was the man on the strength when he was sworn in?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know.

That is
the whole point of the case.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not know whether he
was on the strength for the purposes of getting a pension for disability or not.. I would have to look into the matter. It is a legal question.
Then there is a difference between being on the strength for pension purposes and being on the strength for service, I suppose?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I shall be only too glad
to get the legal officers of my department to give my hon. friend the best legal reply which can be given.

The minister should do
better than that.

I am not going to take this opportunity to make a speech. The Minister of National Defence for Air made a comprehensive statement to the committee, and I do not think there is any doubt in the mind of anyone who listened to him about the job which the air force has performed since its inception; we also have some idea of the task which lies ahead for that particular branch of the service. The only observation I would make in this connection is that it is not good policy to take the position of eulogizing one branch of the service. I believe that if and when the opportunity comes, the army will acquit itself just as creditably as the air force. The same remark applies to our navy. It is merely that the air force has had the first opportunity.
To-night we are dealing particularly with the estimates as tabled by the minister, and,

War Appropriation-Air Services
in accordance with the understanding that we were to take them item by item and discuss them specifically, I shall take up the first item and make a few observations dealing with civil salaries and wages.
I believe the minister is aware that there has been some controversy across the country arising out of complaints, by civilian personnel employed by the air force, as to the cost of living bonus. I have had some correspondence, and I understand that national selective service, unemployment insurance, have made a decision to the effect that civilian personnel employed by the air force in the various camps across the country come under the air force direct in the matter of interpretation as to whether they come under the regular order 5963 or the supplementary order applying directly to this particular branch.
I have a complaint specifically from the airport at Sydney, Nova Scotia. It was handled by the regional war labour board and also by the unemployment insurance commission. The complaint is that the civilian personnel employed at that port were engaged with the understanding at the time they were employed that they were to receive forty-three and a half cents an hour, plus cost of living bonus amounting to something over $18-I believe $18.18-a month. The cost of living bonus has not been provided. The unemployment insurance commission, under date of May 19, 1943, observe that they are unable to determine the exact status from the information submitted and suggest that the question of rate should be taken up direct by the employees concerned with the officer commanding the Royal Canadian Air Force. Quite a number of people are affected, and I rise at this time to bring this point to the minister's attention so that he may make some examination with respect to that particular situation.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: May I ask, did they take it up with the officer in charge?
I understand they did.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: What happened?
There has not been any decision arrived at. It has been a matter of controversy for some months.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend any
correspondence which he can send over to me? I shall be only too glad to look into it.
Yes; I will do that.

There are two matters
under the item before us, namely, that relating to civil salaries and wages, about which I should like to make a few remarks. Before
I do so, may I join in the tributes which have been paid by all hon. members who have spoken to the work which has been done in connection with the organization of the Royal Canadian Air Force, to the men and women in the force, to the families of those who have already made the supreme sacrifice, and to those for whom the present is a very anxious time as they listen to the news from day to day.
The cases to which I would direct the attention of the minister come out of equipment depot No. 7, at Winnipeg. The first case has to do with some forty-two employees who in June of last year were informed that trade tests would shortly be available to them in order that they might seek promotion as civil servants working in that depot. I understand that trade tests were conducted on August 17, and that the employees concerned had been advised in daily routine order 165, which had been issued on July 9, that those who were successful at these examinations would have their promotions made retroactive to July 1, 1942. After a considerable time it turned out that, although the tests were 'held in sufficient time for the increase to be made retroactive to July 1; although the employees had done everything that they were expected to do; although they were assured in daily routine orders that July 1 would be the effective date, still there was delay somewhere along the line, with the result that this matter did not receive the approval of the treasury board until some time after October 1. Accordingly, when the increase was granted it was made retroactive only to October 1 of last year, and the employees were so advised in daily routine order 307 of December 22, 1942. The employees, of course, were rather disappointed, particularly after they had been advised frequently that the effective date would be July 1. Immediately they got in touch with the officers on the station to seek an explanation and to see what should, be done. I shall not take the time of the committee to go into all the details, either as to the explanation or as to what was done, but I may say that these employees 'have been in constant touch with the officers on t'he station and have endeavoured to work through them. In fact, the employees are quite satisfied that the officers in Winnipeg are with them in this matter and that they have done everything in their power to have the increase made effective at the date at which it was promised.
Some time after getting the news that the promise was not to be implemented, the employees were able to have one of their number visit Ottawa during the course of a

War Appropriation-Air Services
trip to the east and take up this matter with the authorities. At that time I was brought in contact with this particular situation, and I have been in quite close touch with it ever since. It was, I believe, in February or March that this representative of these forty-two employees was here. He was in touch with both the civil service commission and the Department of National Defence for Air. The whole story was gone into, and he was assured, both by the chairman of the civil service commission and by the officer in the Department of National Defence for Air, that the matter would be reconsidered. Accordingly, on March 29 of this year, the civil service commission approved an order for making these payments retroactive to July 1 of last year. On the same day, March 29, the approval of the civil service commission was sent to the treasury board. On March 30 the treasury board sent it back to the civil service commission with a request for further information which it felt it should have. The minister will realize what is happening when I give these dates, which are so close to the end of the last fiscal year. The result was that it was April 2 before the civil service commission was able to get back to the treasury board the information asked for on March 30. I emphasize that on March 30 the treasury board acknowledged that it had this matter in hand, because it was on that date that it requested this further information. Matters dragged on until April 22, when the treasury board sent the matter back to the civil service commission again, at this time advising that the change of effective date called for the signature of the Minister of National Defence for Air. I was in touch with the minister as well as with the civil service commission at that time; within a few days the matter was before the minister, and I understand that he signed it. On April 27 the formal application, with the joint approval of the civil service commission and the Minister of National Defence for Air, was again sent to the treasury board. I emphasize the fact that on March 30 the treasury board had had the matter sent back for further information, and that later it asked for the minister's signature. But on May 11, having secured these things the treasury board had asked for, it rejected the application that these payments be made retroactive to July 1.
I must say to the credit of the department that after that date, May 11, I discussed the matter quite fully with one of the officers and that as a result of that discussion the officer agreed with me that the case was one that merited an attempt to have it reconsidered, because the treasury board was apparently rejecting the application on the ground that

it related to the last fiscal year whereas we were now over the line into the new fiscal year. I pointed out that the treasury board had the application for reconsideration on March 30, and that the matter had been hanging fire since last June, July, August and on through the year. I understand, in fact I have a communication to this effect from the department dated May 20, that the matter has again gone to the treasury board, with a request that they reconsider it.
I realize that the minister is familiar with the story, and if he reviews it he will find two or three points, on the basis of which he can say that the responsibility rests upon other shoulders. He can point out that last summer his department was in favour of the effective date being July 1, and that throughout the whole story he has been, or at least his department has been, in favour of the request of the employees. But the problem is still with us.
I do not know how to get at the treasury board; I have not been in the' house long enough to find out. But in view of the fact that this is a matter relating to the civilian employees of the Royal Canadian Air Force* and that the item of money we are now voting is the money that goes to pay civilian em->
ployees, it seems to me that this is the place to raise the question, and I hope the minister will be able to give some statement at least indicating that he and his department are doing their very best to implement this definite promise which was made to this group of employees as indicated by certain daily routine orders that were issued. These employees were amazed on January 22, 1943, when they read in D.R.O. No. 17 of that day that one of their number had had the effective date of her increase changed from October 1, 1942, to July 1, 1942. They did not regret the fact that she was given what they were all asking for, but they found it difficult to understand why it was impossible to do for the rest of the group what had been done for her.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I wish the hon. member would tell me how she worked it. I would do it for the rest.

I am glad to have that statement on the record. I will communicate it to the rest of the group and try to find out. I will give the minister by correspondence the name of the person who was more fortunate than the rest.
There is another matter I should like to discuss with the minister, but perhaps he might like to make a statement first in connection with what I have just brought to his attention.

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know what statement to make. I should like to know how they beat the treasury board. If anyone can tell me, I will throw up both hands and cheer.

Will the minister at least confirm my statement that he and his department agree that the promise made these employees ought to be implemented1 and that he and his department are doing everything possible to that end.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would have to look over the correspondence again, but I take it that my hon. friend's statement is accurate, and if we made a promise we will fight to have it fulfilled. Rut I will not promise that we can beat the treasury board.

The other case to which I wish to refer arises likewise out of No. 7 equipment depot in the city of Winnipeg. This time it relates to a group of more than 200 employees, and I hope that in our discussion we do not have any passing of responsibility such as we had a moment ago in response to some of the remarks of the hon. member for York South. In this case we have a group of more than 200 men who are known as general duty men. They are not classified as civil servants, but they are employees of the Department of National Defence for Air, and I take it that their wages come out of the item which is now under discussion. The matter affecting these employees has its origin at least two years ago, and it is still hanging fire and causing a great deal of discontent and dissatisfaction among these men. There has been some change since they were first hired, but not a great deal. When they were first hired the desire of the department was to engage ' them at forty cents an hour, but it was discovered that the minimum wage or the fair wage provisions in the Manitoba act made it necessary to pay forty-five cents an hour, and that rate was paid. However, when the question of a cost of living bonus came into the picture and it was agreed that the men should get this bonus-let me make this clear -it was added to the forty-five cents which they were then receiving. In other words, they were paid forty-five cents, plus the bonus, for a matter of two or three months; I just forget how long it was. It was then discovered that it was possible to tell these men that before the bonus was paid they were getting forty-five cents an hour only because the provincial law required that they should be paid this rate, but since the cost
of living bonus on top of the lower rate of forty cents would give them a total in excess of the rate demanded by the provincial law-
I notice the minister is laughing, and perhaps it is amusing, if it were not so serious to the men concerned-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is getting pretty complicated for me to follow.
It is complicated, and amusing to some, but it is a serious matter.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know who thought up the reason to keep these men from getting the bonus. He must have been trying very hard.

He must have been a second cousin to the treasury board. Let me go back and line it up again. They were hired at forty-five cents an hour. They were paid this rate not because their employers, the minister's department, wanted to pay it, but because the provincial law required that it should be paid. Then when the bonus was paid-whoever thought up this scheme apparently did not think it up quickly enough, because they got the bonus for two or three months on top of the forty-five cent rate- these men were told that they would have to go back to the forty cent rate as a basic rate, because that rate plus the bonus would give them a little more than forty-five cents and the provincial regulations would thus be met. This happened perhaps two or three years ago and, while there has been considerable change in the personnel, these men have never got over what they felt-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: May I ask what is the situation now?

I was leading up to that point. The situation has been improved in the sense that the basic rate has been increased to forty-five or fifty cents, and the bonus is paid in addition. In a sense the situation has been corrected, but the injustice of the experience has stuck with them and they feel quite discontented and unhappy about the whole thing.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Was that the equipment
depot at Winnipeg?

Yes, No. 7 equipment
depot. At that time I had not become a member of this house, but I was in contact with this situation. These men asked me to see what could be done, and I wrote to one of the members of this group, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), who endeavoured to take it up with the' Minister
War Appropriation-Air Services

of National Defence for Air. I shall not take the time to put the letters on the record, but the minister replied suggesting that the hon. member should get in touch with the Minister of Labour. He did so, and the Minister of Labour replied suggesting that it was really the responsibility of the Minister of National Defence for Air. These men kept after me to give them such information as I was getting, and when I showed them these letters it did not help matters a great deal. After I came to this house I made further inquiries about how these governmental boards were set up, for whom government employees work, who pays them, who decides how much they will be paid and so on.
Have you found out yet?

Not altogether, but I
know	a	lot more	than	I did before I camehere.	However, I	still	have a great deal tolearn. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I did learn that these men are employed by his department and that the money paid them comes out of his estimates. That	is	the item	we	are now considering.So long	as these	men	are not classified as
civil servants but are considered to be general duty or common labourers, the rates paid to them are fixed, not by the minister or his department but by the regulations of the Department of Labour. These men do not think very kindly of the Department of Labour, largely as a result of the experience they had which I have outlined in some detail.
I found out also that if these men could be classified as civil servants, they would still be employees of the Department of National Defence for Air and would receive their pay out of this item, but their rates of pay and working conditions would be set by the civil service commission rather than by the Department of Labour. That cleared up a point in my mind which had not been clear before. I understood that these men were trying to get connected with the civil service commission. They pointed out to me that the work they are doing could hardly be called general duty or common labour. They have a great deal to do with storing and looking after quite valuable equipment. Some of the men have been there for a considerable time, and a large percentage of them are veterans of the last war. They are keenly interested in what they are doing, and they feel they ought to have a higher rating. They have become interested in the possibility of being classified as civil servants.

I took the matter up with the civil service commission. I have admitted already that there is a great deal I have to learn, and I may have made a mistake in going to the civil service commission before I went to the Department of National Defence for Air. I did not consider it to be a terrible mistake, but I have been told that it might have been better if I had made my representations first of all to the Department of National Defence for Air.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The Department of National Defence for Air would have sent them to the civil service commission, so that I thank my hon. friend for taking the short-cut.

I thank the minister for absolving me of having made a serious mistake. The civil service commission explained the rigmarole which I have outlined and indicated that they were prepared to consider this application. Then we went through more rigmarole. The civil service commission has been in touch with the men, and they have been asked to fill out statement of duty forms as to what they are doing so that the civil service commission might draw up a statement showing whether the men would be better off in the civil service or under the Department of Labour, although they are actually in the minister's department. For a time it looked as though we were making pretty good headway, and the men were hopeful that a civil service classification would be granted and their rates would be higher. They would thus be able to forget the unfortunate experience they had when their rates and conditions were under the direction of the Department of Labour.
The upshot of this was that during the Easter recess an official of the civil service commission and an officer of the Department of National Defence for Air visited Winnipeg, I had quite a lengthy interview with them, and they went out and had interviews with the men. I should like to have gone with them at the time, but they advised against it, and whether or not I should have done so, I accepted their advice in the matter. Now I am told that the men were given a hypothetical choice to make. On the one hand they were asked if they would like to continue as unclassified, general duty men at the hourly rate and be given holidays with pay, one week or two weeks, or if they would prefer to become classified as civil servants with a possible reduction' in their total income.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not know anything about this, but my impression is that if they were civil servants they would get holidays with pay and that if they were on the prevailing

War Appropriation-Air Services
rate they would not get holidays with pay. Perhaps my hon. friend has reversed the situation. If they became civil servants they would get holidays with pay. If they were not civil servants they would get the prevailing daily rate and would not get any pay while they were not working. Am I not right in that?
The minister is making the very criticism of this proposal that was made to these men that I was about to make.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know anything about this particular case, but for twenty-five years I have been fighting to get similar privileges for people in my constituency and have not succeeded. I understood that if one remained on prevailing rates one was not paid for holidays, whereas if one became a civil servant payment went on for the period of the holidays, one week or two weeks. If there is any change in that rule I do not know about it.

That was exactly my understanding of it, and it was the understanding of the men to whom the proposition was put. I am quite sure the proposition was made in the way I have stated; as a matter of fact it was discussed with me in the interview 1 had with the two officials.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: How could they pay people on prevailing rates if they did not work, if they were on holidays?
That was my question.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
This is a new one on me.
I do not understand it.

But that is what the
men were asked, if they would like to continue on the hourly rate and have a concession which they could not possibly realize, or if they would prefer to become civil servants at a rate which was indicated by the officers as lower than actually it might be. The men feel that the proposition which was put to them was deliberately distorted in order to get them to say that they would prefer to remain on the hourly rate.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not know anything
about it, but I hardly think a responsible officer of the civil service commission would make an offer that was not bona fide, at any rate. I should be surprised if he did, and1 I would draw it to the attention of the civil service commission if that were done.

If the minister will look into the matter I think he will find that he should draw it to the attention of an officer of his own department. If my information is
correct, and I have reason to believe it is, it was the air force officer who made the proposal with the official of the civil service commission standing by. If I may try to state their case, these men feel that the department does not want them to be classified, that the choice was deliberately distorted so that they would choose the alternative the department wanted them to choose.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that I do not care; I am all in favour of their getting increased rates. We are not trying to distort anything, so far as the department is concerned.

May I say further that
if the statement just made by the minister inr dicates his view on the matter-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am afraid that will not
help my hon. friend. I have been fighting the civil service commission and treasury board ever since I have been a member of this house, and I have been here since 1917, but it has not done me any good.

I am still of the opinion that if the minister or the department would like to have these men classified, the civil service commission is ready to classify them, but that actually the officers in the minister's department are not sympathetic. They have given me their reasons for not being sympathetic, though I need not take time to give those reasons.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I should like to know them.

Since the minister has
asked for them, they feel that there will be problems related to getting overtime work out of the men if they are classified as civil servants instead of being on an hourly rate. That is the principal objection that was raised.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I was under the impression
that it was just the opposite, that when you are in the civil service you do overtime work, but that if you are on a prevailing rate of pay you get time and a half for overtime.

At least one officer in
the minister's department feels that there would be difficulty in persuading the men to work, even though civil service regulations say they may have to, after having been paid for it. He also felt that there would be difficulty as between these civilians and the service personnel. I am glad to hear the minister's statement, despite his feeling that it will not do any good. I am glad he is for a civil service classification in a case like this; and if

War Appropriation-Air Services
he will go ahead and battle this thing through, from, my talks with the officials of the civil service commission. I have reason to believe that something can be done. Let me make this comparison. In the other case about which I was talking, the case of the forty-two whose promotion was made effective on the wrong date, the department was on the side of the employees, while the civil service commission did not stand up for them at first, although later it agreed with their request. In this case, however, the civil service commission has already indicated to me its willingness to go ahead and classify these men, certainly if the department asks for it. I may repeat that it was at a fairly late stage of the proceedings that I was told that the attitude of the Department of National Defence for Air toward this whole matter might have been more sympathetic if it had come about either through my going to the department or through the men making that approach, but that my having gone to t'he civil service commission-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend will
disabuse his mind of that idea. I have not the slightest objection to his going over my head to the civil service commission at any time.
I am glad to have that statement from the minister. Now it is on record, and I should be able to use it if ever I am told that sort of thing again.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: You bet.

I am now told that conditions are getting a little worse. For a considerable length of time the personnel of this group of over two hundred did not change a great deal, but lately the personnel has begun to change quite considerably. I am told that every day men are resigning or are being discharged and are being replaced the next day with other men sent over in response to applications made to selective service; in fact, the selective service office at Winnipeg is now beginning to wonder at the turnover at this place. The men themselves are wondering whether this rapid change in personnel, which occurs partly because the men are getting fed up and leaving and partly because some are being discharged, is an attempt to break up this group which has been struggling in this matter for about two yearn. They wonder what is happening, and are becoming quite discouraged. As I have already indicated, I have been in touch with this matter for at least a year and a half; and these men have been in touch with the Department of National
iMr. Knowles. 1
Defence for Air and the Department of Labour for about two years. And yet through all this time this matter has never before been brought up in the house or in committee. An attempt has been made to deal with the matter direcly with the department. That has been my aim right along.
