But I feel the thing has reached the stage where it is necessary to say something about it in a more public way, and to express here the hope that the minister will do what he can to fight this case. I do not share the sense of futility he seems to have as to the effectiveness of his activities in the matter. I. believe that if I can enlist his support on behalf of these men, despite what he says some good will come of it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I shall be glad to help all
I can against the civil service commission at any time. I moved for its abolition on three occasions in this house.
This is a serious matter.

Reverting to the discussion raised a little while ago by the hon. member for Bow River, may I point out that the minister seemed to focus his attention on the point as to whether or not that particular case was one for the pension board. I am not going to discuss the case, but I believe that a principle worthy of some clarification is involved.
As an illustration I shall present a set of circumstances to the minister. The young man in question is, we will say, around the age of nineteen years. Recognizing that he may be called into the services, he enlists in the air force. But he does not wish to be called immediately. The fact is that he is not called, but enlists and obtains his number. Them- and I do not know whether I am using the proper term-his file is put back, and there is a general understanding between him and the recruiting officer that he will not be called until a certain date. After that, should he be checked by the mounted police-and that is not likely-he has in his pocket documents showing that he has enlisted. Then the time arrives when the air force calls him to the service. Five or six months may have elapsed between his date of enlistment and the date he is called up and sent to the manning depot, or to the training centre. Is this young man considered to be in the air force at the time of his original enlistment?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

I will leave the case mentioned by the hon. member for Bow River in the hands of the minister and the hon. member. The statement is, however, that this young man is now enlisted, and on strength.

War Appropriation-Air Services
Would the minister make a statement with respect to decorations, awards, medals and the like given to members of the air force who have rendered outstanding service? I ask the question because I am under the impression that usually awards are given to those men in the air force who have commissions, or who are in higher ranks, and may have better opportunities to distinguish themselves. The mere fact that they are in positions of authority may win them awards, whereas those who serve under the officers-wireless air gunners, air gunners or men of lower rank, but serving in aircrew - do not seem to receive the same distinctions. The country would like to have a statement from the minister. I was asked about this matter by a man well known in public life. How are these awards granted? On what basis are they given, and what process is followed in giving them?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The question of awards is a difficult and complex one. I cannot answer the hon. member offhand as to how awards are given. I suppose he is aware that overseas awards for gallantry are usually granted on the recommendations of a commanding officer. Then, through a routine process the recommendation reaches the higher authorities. Awards other than awards for specific acts of gallantry-these are periodic awards-but for service over an extended period, and not necessarily including acts of gallantry, are usually given upon recommendation of the commanding officer of the command, group, unit or whatever the formation may be. Beyond that I am afraid I cannot go into detail, because I have never looked into the matter carefully. However, I shall do so, and I shall be glad to give the hon. member all the information I can to-morrow.
There are several points I should like to mention, but first may I say that as I look across the floor of the chamber I see my old friend who is commonly known as "Chubby" Power.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Tut, tut!

I think "Chubby" Power is well named. We all have the greatest respect for him. As a matter of fact the country wishes it had three "Chubby" Powers in the House of Commons, instead of one, and that they could be in charge of the three defence departments. The minister, as a matter of fact, is more or less human-and that is something not peculiar to ministers. Most ministers I have known have not been human at all, except, of course, the Minister of Pensions and National Health. Sometimes he is human, too. But they are the only
two in the cabinet who are any good, anyway. You could wash all the rest out-and that is what the public thinks, too. The rest of the cabinet are just a wash-out; but these two are pretty good. I have not had enough experience with the parliamentary assistants to express any opinion, but we shall get to know them, just the same as we know the ministers.
I have one or two observations to make which may be worth while. First of all, I take off my hat to these gallant boys of the air force. But in all our armed forces we have the youth of Canada who are equally impressed with a sense of their duty and each of them will do his duty when the opportunity comes. Canada's air force has done a marvellous job for Canada but it has had more opportunity. I am sure that when the army gets its opportunity it will give just as good account of itself as all our other forces. I do not think it is quite right for us to eulogize one force and not pay tribute to the other branches of the service as well. Of course, we all realize that when our air force is on a bombing raid over Europe the sacrifice of one of our pilots might mean the saving of possibly ten thousand lives. I want the minister to listen to me for a moment.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am listening.
I did not catch the minister's eye. These boys of the air force are all young. You have picked out the best of the whole crowd.-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Well, you have just picked them out, that is all, but equally fine young men have been picked for the army and navy, too. They are all young, and what I wish to know is this. After the war is over, what do you propose to do about giving these young men the university training .they otherwise might have had. What opportunities will you give them to carry on and make their way in life?
I should also like some information about transfers from the Royal Air Force to the Royal Canadian Air Force. A great many lads who were turned down by the Royal Canadian Air Force in the early days went over to England and joined the Royal Air Force. Some of them now want to transfer to the Royal Canadian Air Force. I hope the minister will give some information on that question. Another question that arises is that of seniority. What positions are they to have? How is seniority to be worked for them in so far as the permanent force is concerned and so far as the temporary force or whatever you like to call it is concerned?
War Appropriation-Air Services

The Minister of Agriculture the other day said that rumours had come to his ears of extravagance on messes. I must say that I, too, heard something about extravagances and so on. But when you look into it you find that where there is a fairly nice mess, whether in the air force, the army or the navy, somebody donated all this stuff. No question like the extravagances we heard about in connection with rugs enters into the matter at all. Some people when they see a nice mess get the idea that there is extravagance and that everything is cockeyed. But the truth is that very often the equipment has been donated.
I should like to know what we are doing about gliders in Canada. Are we doing anything in connection with gliders?
I think the people of Canada would also like to know something about our activities in connection with the United States air force in Alaska.
I should like to know something about air defence in the St. Lawrence. I do not know whether the minister is free to tell us anything about that, but it is a subject in which the public is interested.
Do we propose to have a fleet air arm in Canada? Can the minister tell us something about that?
What about the standards for enlistment at the present time? What are the requirements?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The physical standards?

The physical standards, the educational standards, qualifications as to age and so forth. What enlistments do we require in the air force to-day? Do we need any more ground crew, repair men, and so forth? The minister knows what I mean. -
I should be glad if the minister would tell us something about equipment depots. What personnel is required for an equipment depot? Where are our equipment depots? What do they do?
There is also the question of financial responsibility for the Royal Air Force in Canada and the Royal Canadian Air Force overseas. Are the pay and allowances for the Royal Air Force in Canada on the same basis in Canada as for the Royal Canadian Air Force in Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The answer to that is yes right away.

The pay and allowances are the same? O.K. I think I

have now all my questions off my chest except the question of commissions for our air force. The minister has already been asked several questions about that. I do see an incongruity, and this happens in certain cases, in having a sergeant-pilot taking a bomber over Germany with a pilot officer or a flying officer as part of his crew. I do not know how that works out, but I do know that it has happened on many occasions. My personal opinion is that all these men who go into the air, after they have had a certain number of flights, should automatically become officers if they qualify. Perhaps the minister would make a statement on that.
One last word. I wish to pay tribute to all those men of Canada in the Royal Canadian Air Force who are doing such a magnificent job and to all those who unfortunately have lost their lives in the service of their country. Their names will live forever. Too much cannot be said for what they have done for Canada.
Perhaps when the minister makes his statement he would tell us the number of Canadians in the Royal Air Force and in the Royal Canadian Air Force who have lost their lives or been wounded or made prisoners of war. I congratulate the minister, not for himself, but for all those fine men in the Royal Canadian Air Force who have such a wonderful sense of duty and are doing such a marvellous job so far as Canada is concerned.

I have only two questions, and I shall be quite brief. I ask them now, although I do not see any item in this break-down of the minister's estimates which they come under.
First, may I join with many other hon. members who have spoken this evening in expressing appreciation of the valour and self-sacrifice of the splendid young men and women whom we have in the Canadian air force. Had I the time I would tell of the splendid type of enlistments in that part of the province of Saskatchewan which I represent. Not only are they qualified from the point of view of education, but physically they are splendid men. I regret to have to say that many from our own community have already made the supreme sacrifice. No doubt the Royal Canadian Air Force will play a very important part in the months to come in the winning of the war.
We have listened this evening, as we did while the estimates of the Minister of National Defence (Army) were before the

War Appropriation-Air Services
committee, to various hon. members bringing individual cases before the minister. I think a great deal of time could be saved if, instead of putting these cases before the minister while he is sitting in committee, hon. members would bring them to the attention of the proper officers of his department. Rules and regulations have been adopted for the guidance of each branch of the armed services, and if hon. members will acquaint themselves with the conditions governing promotions, salaries, salary increases and pensions, and then will carry on their inquiries in the correct way, by going to the proper authorities, they could save us a lot of time. I will say this for the minister who is before us this evening, that they will get action. I have taken three or four cases to him. In one case we got action so fast that the man concerned obtained his postponement and was out of the air force before he realized it. I appreciate that the air force must be governed by rules and regulations, and I repeat that if hon. members will study them and follow the right procedure they will soon obtain the information they require and will be able to advise those who write such letters as we have heard so much about to-night.
I have two questions to ask the minister. One of the young men in my locality is a prisoner of war. He was in England when the war broke out, joined the Royal Air Force, and was taken prisoner. He would now like to transfer to the Royal Canadian Air Force, and I wish to know from the minister how he can go about having a transfer made. He has made representations through certain authorities, but without getting satisfaction, and he would like to have the application definitely dealt with.
Another subject to which I would invite the minister's attention relates to cases of men-I have two particularly in mind-who were killed while serving in the air force. They were industrious chaps and had opened a savings account in a bank in England. Their parents are unable to get any action with respect to the transfer of these accounts. One of the cases is of six months' standing, and one family which is concerned with this question has three sons in the air force, one of whom has already paid with his life.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That is the estate of a
deceased?
Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I must say that earlier in the war there was a great deal of confusion and it took months and months to get estates settled. But only two or three days ago I
inquired as to the progress in settling estates, and I am informed that over two thousand had been already settled and another fourteen or fifteen hundred are well on the way to settlement. I will get these figures for my hon. friend. If he will let me know the particulars to which he refers we will cable to England.
I do not think the parents are so anxious for an immediate settlement that that is necessary.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
As I say, there was a great deal of delay at the start, but I know things are being hastened.
The other question, regarding the transfer of a prisoner of war to the Royal Canadian Air Force, is really a poser. I never contemplated that, and I do not think I can do much about it.

I wish to bring to the attention of the committee and the minister the matter of getting compassionate leave for some members of aircrews. It seems to be settled policy that a member of an aircrew cannot get leave or be released from the service under any circumstances whatever. It happens that conditions in the homes of some of these people-I have farm homes particularly in mind'-change rapidly, and I have learned of some very unfortunate cases. One I have in mind is that of a young man, an only son, who enlisted in goodi faith. His father has been taken seriously ill; yet it is quite impossible for the young man to obtain a long enough leave to go back to the farm and carry on until the farm and the stock can be sold or some other arrangement made.
I quite realize that it costs a good deal of money to educate a man in an aircrew. I realize, too, that these boys are doing wonderful work and are badly needed at the present time. But it is most discouraging for some to find that farm help cannot be obtained and that although their families are suffering very severe financial loss they cannot get leave to go home. It seems to me that often the commanding officers to whom applications are made are not very sympathetic. Sometimes the file is missing; weeks and months go by, and the lads become discouraged and feel that the sacrifices which they are asked to undertake are out of all proportion. Could the minister not suggest some way whereby leave could be granted for at least a number of months, or the boy be allowed to get out of the service altogether where desperate conditions have arisen in the family which would make compassionate release seem justified.

In connection with this item we are discussing, I wish to ask the minister
War Appropriation-Air Services

a question somewhat along the lines of those of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I speak with some trepidation after the remarks of the member for Qu'Appelle, who advised us not to ask the minister questions and then asked a few himself. My question is with regard to the variation in the rates of pay for ordinary service men at Trenton air station. The men whose case I am discussing are not receiving cost of living bonus.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Civilians?

Yes. They advise me that there are men on the staff who do receive cost of living bonus. The men in particular to whom I refer work long hours, as high as ninety a week, and they have not been able to get a satisfactory disposition of their claims. That is the question I wish to put to the minister with regard to civilian employees.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will look into it.
Following what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has said, I have had a number of cases in regard to airmen who have been killed and whose estates it has taken months to settle.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend, but I made inquiries only a few days ago and they said the situation was better.
Have they a new system of checking, or is it due to the fact that the officers in charge have not been reporting these cases properly or sending them here? I have received letters-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I imagine it is better
organized, and the fact that we are having a hand in it might account for the improvement.
If you had a hand in it, it would be better.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I mean, the Royal Canadian Air Force having a hand in it overseas, which they did not have at that time.

This
is also in regard1 to Newfoundland. I am thinking of the fire there. In Peterborough we had a man who was burnt to death.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We cannot blame it on
anyone but the R.C.A.F., but if there is anything wrong we want to know.
This case has not been settled, and it was said1 that the facts had not been sent to Ottawa.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Will the hon. member send me the details?
Yes.

There is some information
under this item and the next which I should like to obtain. Will the minister furnish the number of civilian personnel and the number of air personnel employed by his director of public information, or publicity department, during the past fiscal year or up to any subsequent date, and will he let us know how this personnel is distributed by provinces or by military districts, also the number in Great Britain, if any, and the number in the United States? Will the minister furnish us also with the total wages and salaries paid to civilian personnel and air personnel who are employed in his publicity department or by the director of public relations? Will he give also the total travelling expenses and all other costs and expenses that were paid to these civilian personnel and service personnel during the past fiscal year or up to any subsequent date? Will he let us know also how many of the personnel, both civilian and service, in this branch of his department receive salaries over $5,000, if any; how many receive salaries of $4,000 or more; how many receive salaries of $3,000-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I will give all the salaries.
Why ask for $4,000 or $5,000? We will give them all from nothing up. I was under the impression that these questions had been made an order for return already. I am not sure.
If they have, I have not seen them.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Anyway, I will give them.

Under civil salaries and wages, may I ask the minister whether or not the bomber command comes within the purview of the operations of the Royal Canadian Air Force? My understanding at the moment is that it does not, but I was wondering whether in the civil salaries and wages here the bomber command actually came within the purview of the department.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The ferry command?
That is what I mean.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have nothing to do with that.

As a matter of information, under whose jurisdiction is it? I should not say the bomber comand, nor is ferry command the right term; transport command is the actual designation in the income tax act. Who is it that provides the salaries for these men, and under whose jurisdiction does the transport command operate?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It is absolutely independent of the R.C.A.F. We have no control or juris-

War Appropriation-Air Services
diction; we have nothing to do with pay or anything else. It is the government of Great Britain.
When the minister says the government of Great Britain, does he mean that the Royal Air Force of Great Britain has control?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend all the details. The ferry command started as the B.O.A.C., the British Overseas Aircraft Corporation. I do not remember what the name was, but it got mixed up with the Canadian Pacific Railway, who furnished pilots and a great number of personnel, and after that it was taken over by the R.A.F. ferry command under Sir Frederick Bowhill in the last two or three months. They formed it into the transport command, with different branches, and it is controlled1 by the British government. We have nothing to do with it except that frequently we furnish personnel to the ferry command and they ferry bombers overseas to do work for them.

Supplementary to what the minister says, when the Royal Canadian Air Force provides personnel for the transport command, are these particular personnel under the rates of pay of the Royal Canadian Air Force, or do they participate in the higher rate of pay of civilians in connection with the transport command?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: So far as I know they are still under R.C.A.F. rates of pay. I do not think they get a higher rate of pay.
If that is the case-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We do not pay them.
-what you have, then, is some men ferrying bombers across at Royal Canadian Air Force rates of pay which are proportionately a good deal lower than those of the transport command?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I believe that was one of the reasons why the Canadian Pacific came into the business. They employed a great many Americans and were paying them $2,000 a month, as against Royal Air Force or Royal Canadian Air Force men who were getting $150 a month. They figured they had to get these men to perform that job of work. We have had nothing to do with that. That was entirely a responsibility of the British government, and I must say that a great many of the boys who were taking the same risk and doing the same job did not like to get ordinary rates of pay. I understand that now the rates of pay for civilian ferry pilots who work
alongside Royal Air Force or Royal Canadian Air Force men are a great deal less than they were originally.

In reference to another subject matter, the minister will recall that two years ago he, as minister, and his department conceived the idea that probably like services in the Department of National Defence for the army and navy, and even for pensions and national health, might coordinate their efforts by convening all the heads of such services as medical services and hospitalization where the type of work was much the same. I will admit that they did not have much success or did not carry out the idea originated by the Minister of National Defence for Air. No one was placed at the head of this coordination committee. Perhaps between now and to-morrow when the minister is to make his reply he will look into the matter and see what has been done to appoint a head of this coordination committee and have it called at the proper time. I am also anxious to know if a secretariat has been set up for this committee so that minutes and records may be kept of what they are able to do. If this committee is not functioning or cannot function for some reason or another, I should like to know. I realize that sometimes it is difficult for men in blue to associate with men in khaki; one service finds it is hard to attend on the other. I was hoping that something would develop from the minister's original idea which 1 thought was sound and which I felt would save this country many thousands of dollars. He will recall that the plan covered not only the three armed services but also certain branches of the Department of Pensions and National Health. A short statement as to where the matter stands would, I am sure, be appreciated by the committee.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The committee on hospitalization is functioning, and functioning extremely well. At present all four medical services are represented, the armed services, and pensions and national health. It is headed up by Colonel Currie, of the Department of National Defence. There is no hospitalization scheme or anything connected with hospitalization that goes through the treasury board or privy council, or is submitted to the ministers without being submitted to this committee. It is one committee that is working extremely well and it sits almost every day.
Does its work cover the medical services?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: So far as I know, the committee has nothing to do with medical services.

War Appropriation-Air Services
It was really constituted to see that hospital facilities across the country were not duplicated.

How long has it been
functioning?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It was started about two
years ago. I do not know when it really struck its stride, but it is in its stride now.

Following the
matter of medical services is the question of medical supplies. As the Minister of Pensions and National Health knows, there is a duplication in connection with those responsible for providing supplies for the different hospital units. The Minister of Pensions and National Health is fortunate in having a service which has been built up over two or three decades and is in good working order. However, the department which has to do with medical supplies for the air defence and the department that has to do with supplies for the army have been in a deplorable tangle. I was hoping that the tangle might have been straightened out by coordinating the different branches which are handling the same supplies.
If the minister feels so disposed, perhaps he will enlarge upon his statement and place a deposition on the record in connection with medical supplies. The supplies run into many millions of dollars, particularly when you get into X-ray equipment and equipment of other types. Undoubtedly there has been considerable duplication. I hesitate to say it, but the supplies branch of the Department of Pensions and National Health apparently are not aware of the working of the supplies branch of the army. One is situated across from the Chateau Laurier, the other being on Kent street, and there does not seem to be any cooperation between these particular units. The department for air was not organized with regard to supplies.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The army purchases all our supplies with the exception of special equipment, such as X-ray equipment.

The view is
taken in England, and perhaps it is quite sound, that air should handle hospitalization connected with the physical endurance which must be undergone by members of the air force. These men face particular hazards, quite different from those faced by men in the army. In that view I concur. I agree with the extent of the hospitalization which has to do with the peculiar operations of the Department of National Defence for Air, but when it comes to dealing with the ordinary

sicknesses to which we are all subject I think there should be the maximum cooperation to provide the maximum service at a minimum cost.
For the information of the minister I would say that there seems to be a tendency on the part of his department to set up an organization to deal with all phases of this work, quite apart from the special hazards of his branch of the service. As I say, there could be considerably more cooperation, and those in the minister's department who are charged with this responsibility should be encouraged to cooperate to the fullest and enlarge their activities only in connection with the special hazards of their particular service rather than to try to enlarge them to cover the entire field of hospitalization.
Many of these men find themselves located in small communities. While up Goderich way, I had the pleasure of the company of half a dozen of the young men from the field there over the week-end. They tell me that they have to get hospital treatment and medical supplies in a small community in Huron county. I suggest to the minister that he encourage his medical officers and those charged with this responsibility to use, where-ever possible, the local facilities instead of setting up too many expensive units here and there across the country.
Would the people employed at the privately-owned training schools come within this item of civilian salaries and wages?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They would come under
civilian schools.

The item in the army
estimates covering civilian salaries and wages for this year amounted to a little over $9,000,000, whereas the similar item for the air force comes to some $18,500,000. I think by way of clarification the minister ought to indicate the main items that would be responsible for such an increase, having regard to the difference in size as between the two forces.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not know just how
many civilians the army have in their employ, but we have somewhere between fifteen and sixteen thousand. I will say to my hon. friend that very early in my career as a minister I insisted that as far as possible where one could get a civilian to do the work, one should do so rather than get a service man. I preferred that. As time went on, it became impossible to get civilians and I have had to

War Appropriation-Air Services
use more service men, so that probably we have proportionately more civilians in our employ than they have in the army.
Then is it fair to assume that the average rates of pay of those engaged as civilian personnel are higher than the rates of those in the service generally?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The average civilian rate is
$1,210 per annum. So far as civilians are concerned, if they are casual labour or what we call exempt positions from the civil service commission; they are employed at the rates prevailing in the locality. Otherwise they are under civil service rates, whatever they may be, for that particular class of work. There is no difference between our rates of pay for civil servants and those of any other department. Perhaps seventy-five out of the whole fifteen thousand were appointed directly by order in council. The remainder are under the civil service or in a class which is exempt as casual labour.
Has the minister adopted this policy largely as an economic measure, or was there any other reason?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Early in the game I felt
that sooner or later there would be criticism in this house and in the country if a very large number of people in uniform were doing work that could be done just as well by civil servants. I held to that theory until such time as we could no longer get civilians; then it was necessary to use service personnel. It was really from a political point of view as much as any other; I do not think the question of saving money entered into it, because I do not believe there is very much difference.

What is the practice with
regard to the civilians who are employed at the different air stations? Do they take an oath of allegiance, or what is the provision in that regard?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am told that they do
take an oath of allegiance.
I suppose they come and go a great deal?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

I understand, for example,
that at some of the stations many civilian waitresses are employed.
Mr. POWER; I would not think so, at any of our service stations. There may be some at the civilian training schools; I would not know about that. At nearly all our service stations the waitresses are members of the women's division of the air force.

What about the training
stations?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They are all under contract with the department; they look after the food and everything else.
Mr. Green:	But they have civilian
waitresses at the training stations?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I would not know whether
or not they have civilian waitresses, but I would suspect so.
Is it the intention to replace those waitresses by members of the women's division?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, not at contract schools. These civilian training schools are operated on a contract basis; we just pay them the contract fee of so much.
I do not mean the civilian training schools; I mean the training stations operated by the air force.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think we have any civilian waitresses; I cannot think of any at our own service schools. We would have a great many of the women's division of the R.C.A.F. They are in the service; they are enlisted.
But no civilian waitresses?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think we have any; I should be very much surprised if we had.

Then may I ask whether under this item covering civil salaries and wages will come the provision for the new R.C.A.F. cafeterias in Ottawa, about which we see so much in the newspapers from time to time? Perhaps in view of the minister's keen interest in this matter and his desire to give the committee information on these points, he would not mind saying a word to the committee now with respect to the position in which the air force now finds itself.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I really do not know just what I can tell the committee that they have not read over and1 over again, rightly or wrongly, accurately or inaccurately, in the Ottawa newspapers.
Perhaps we should have an accurate account.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Perhaps you had better get it from the newspapers; they seem to know far more about it than the minister does. We were operating a cafeteria for our employees, both civilian and service, in the Lisgar building.

That is the building out near the farm?
3250

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No; the one in the Lisgar building; the other one was not to be taken over until to-day, I think, or to-morrow. In the Lisgar building, where headquarters is located, the service was performed by service personnel, and for that reason the cost was comparatively low in comparison with that of similar meals outside. Then it happened that trouble developed at No. 5 temporary budding, near the farm, and I understood we were asked' to care for our nine hundred employees there. We undertook to do so in the same way that we were operating the cafeteria in the Lisgar building.
In other words, by air force personnel?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes. After some discussion as to the prices to be charged it was decided that in order to be fair to everyone and so that there would be no discrimination later on, when the government policy with respect to cafeterias generally in Ottawa is developed, for the time being the same prices would prevail at the farm and at the Lisgar building as had prevailed hitherto; that is, comparatively low prices at the Lisgar building and prices somewhat higher at the farm. These will remain in force until about June 20 or June 21, at which time comparisons will be made, and it will be our endeavour to see whether the prices cannot coincide, to some extent, and to ascertain the real costs of carrying on these operations.
You do not know yet whether you are losing or making money?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think on the straight cost of the food alone I am not losing much in the Lisgar building; I do not know whether I am making much either. At the other building, with all services furnished free, so to speak, by the R.C.A.F., I rather imagine some money would be made. I am not sure, though;
I am not very familiar with this matter. I learned most of it from the newspapers.
A moment ago the minister mentioned a general policy on the part of the government with respeot to cafeterias.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is being developed now.
Did I understand the minister to say that this policy has already been defined?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is under very serious consideration, and I imagine the results of these two experiments will foe taken into consideration before a policy is defined.
Does this mean that the government has in mind eventually providing a cafeteria service for its employees in Ottawa generally?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think they have in mind some attempt to solve the difficulty of obtaining meals at the present time, under my hon. friend the Minister of Pensions and National Health, who will endeavour to obtain the best kind of nutrition at the lowest possible cost to civil servants generally, and particularly the low paid civil servants. I am speaking only in broad terms, because I know it has been a matter of consideration by the government for some time, but I do not know that any policy has been defined. The experiments now being carded on in these two locations will, I imagine, have some bearing on the solution.

Some move has been made to meet the housing problem here, but I do not want to give the government too much commendation because I fancy there is still a great deal to be done. Having in mind the problem connected with workers in Ottawa, and in view of the terrific overcrowding in this capital city, it seems to me the next logical move would be one in connection with feeding of employees. I think everyone is pretty well agreed that the conditions under which most people in Ottawa have to take their meals in the downtown area are not very satisfactory. All one needs to do is to walk along the streets of Ottawa and see the situation for himself. Those who suffer most are the ones who have only a limited noon hour. It is all right for the person who has a long time to spend at an eating house, but for those who have only a short time between the time they leave their work and the time they must come back it seems to me there is a crying need for some relief. Every hon. member sees them attempting as best they can to line up, grab a sandwich and a cup of coffee. They are lucky if they can get that much before it is time to go back to work.

Would the minister
bring down additional information regarding these civilian employees? I believe he has already been asked to give information respecting their salaries and wages, and possibly as to the number.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can give the number right away.

What I want-possibly the minister can give it, and possibly not- is a break-down showing how many of them are in civil service classifications and how many are exempt.

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think I have that information, too.
That will be fine.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have 15,324. The average rate, including bonus, is $1,210. Appointments to all positions which might, in the opinion of the civil service commission, be classified under the Civil Service Act are legalized by the civil service commission. Positions exempt from the Civil Service Act; that is, exempt by law-
If it is exempt by the act, it is exempt by law.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Civilians are employed in prevailing rate positions at Royal Canadian Air Force units to conduct maintenance work. This class of employee is utilized as firemen, mechanics, skilled and unskilled labourers, and so on, who are paid wages in accordance with the minimum wage schedule issued by the national war labour board. The department is authorized by order in council P.C.48-2105, dated March 16, 1943, to engage such personnel as may be required for the building, renovating, remodelling and maintenance of buildings and landing fields at Royal Canadian Air Force projects, such personnel to exclude professional, technical and clerical employees.
The selection of personnel is made through the national selective service offices in the various localities and, prior to the inception of national selective service, the provincial employment bureaus.
In appointment of specialist services for technical and administrative duties, selection is made from private industry, appointment effected by individual order in council, which is referred in each case to the civil service commission for consideration.
Since the inception of the department in 1940, a total of seventy-five appointments by individual orders in council have been effected; forty-two of the personnel were 'seconded to the department from private industry; thirteen construction personnel for employment in Newfoundland; seven stenographers for appointment in Washington, and thirteen direct appointments. Fourteen of the seventy-five personnel have completed their respective assignment, and the employment has been discontinued, leaving the net appointments by orders in council still on the strength of the department at sixty-one.
I think I have a list of the different types of employees, and that list could be put on Hansard. I have the information with respect to civilian personnel employed at headquar-

ters, although I have not that information with me. I can place on Hansard, for my hon. friend's information, a full list of civilian employees, and the number in each category or class.
The minimum I should like to have from the minister-and if he wishes to give more I should be glad to get it -would be to break that 15,000 into three groups-those appointed by orders in council-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is seventy-five.

Sixty-one, net. Then, I would want those who are classified as civil servants, and those who are exempt. And then would he give the average wage of each of those three groups? The minister has already given the average for the 15,000. Let us have the average for each of the three groups I have indicated.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Perhaps I can get together the wages paid to each particular trade in each group. Would that be what the hon. member wishes-carpenters, and so on?

I should like to have
that, but I have hesitated to ask for it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know whether I could get that information, but that is what the hon. member wants.
I should like to get it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will see whether it can be obtained.

Reverting to the question of cafeterias, may I congratulate the minister upon any effort which he might have put forth to render available at reasonable prices good and substantial meals to the people concerned? I believe much more attention must be paid by the government to the matter of giving employees, who are working for incomes far too small, and who are being [DOT] taxed far too much, substantial meals at rates as low as possible, so that they may be able to save a dollar or two.
Are the civil employees at the air training stations given the cost of living bonus, the same as private industry would pay in that locality?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Just the same as any other civilian employees.

Whether they are employed by the government or not, they are given the same bonus as private industry would pay in that locality?
The King's Birthday

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know just what the civil service bonus is, as compared with the bonus paid by the individual employers, outside. I cannot give information on that point, but I can have it checked. That is a matter for the civil service commission and the treasury board. But I understand there is a rate of bonuses given to civil servants throughout the country, and I do not think they vary much.
The civil service would affect only those who are civil service appointees.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Those under the control of the civil service commission. And those who are performing work which exempts them from the Civil Service Act get the same bonus as those who are employed by individual employers, I assume.
If hon. members would be prepared to have the item pass, I shall be only too glad to make replies to questions as to civilian employees.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
